Ulaştırma ve Altyapı Bakanı Abdulkadir Uraloğlu, Hızlı Geçiş Sistemi’nde (HGS) icra yoluyla alınan usulsüz ödemelerin iade edileceğini belirtti.
HGS’de özel otoyollarda ihlalli geçiş ödemesinin yapılmasına veya sürücülerin hesabında yeterli bakiye olmasına rağmen icra takibiyle karşı karşıya kalınması son günlerde şikayet konusuydu.
Uraloğlu, 20 Kasım’da ‘söz konusu icra takiplerinin toplam geçişlerin yalnızca yüzde 0,43’ünü oluşturduğu ‘nu öne sürerek HGS icralarının durdurulduğunu duyurmuştu .
22 Kasım’da Adalet Bakanı Akın Gürlek’se İstanbul başsavcılığının soruşturma başlattığını duyurmuş, haksız borçlandırma iddialarının araştırıldığını açıklamıştı.
Konu dün Ulaştırma ve Altyapı Bakanlığı’nın TBMM Plan ve Bütçe Komisyonu’ndaki 2027 bütçe görüşmelerinde gündeme geldi. Uraloğlu, usulsüz ödemelerin iade edileceğini söyledi.
Özel otoyollarda yaklaşık 2,2 milyon geçişin takibe alındığını belirten Uraloğlu yasal takibin kamu alacağı olmadığı için kanuna göre yapıldığı bilgisini paylaştı:
“ HGS aboneliği olan bir araç otoyola girdikten sonra HGS etiketi okunuyor. Eğer etiket okunmuyorsa plaka okunarak HGS etiketiyle eşleştiriliyor. Hesapta yeterli bakiye varsa geçiş ücreti otomatik tamamlanıyor. Eğer ihlalli geçiş varsa 15 güne kadar her türlü ödeme cezasız olarak yapılabilmektedir. 15 güne kadar eğer bir ödeme yapılmamışsa 45 güne kadar bir kat cezayla ödeme yapılmaktadır. Yine 45 günden sonra ödeme yapılmamışsa bu sefer yasal takip süreci başlatılmaktadır.
Biz e-Devlet’ten artık firmaların inisiyatifine bırakmaksızın hangi günlerde, hangi yöntemlerle uyarı yapacağımızın kararını aldık. TÜRKSAT’ımıza bunu yaptırıyoruz.
Karayolları Genel Müdürlüğü üzerinden 2025’te 584 milyon, özel otoyollardan 516 milyon geçiş yapılmış. Kara yollarında cezasız esasında ödeme yüzde 88’ken özel otoyollarda yüzde 97. Burada cezai yaptırımlar biraz ağır olduğu için ödeme istekliliği birazcık daha fazla.
Yaklaşık 2,2 milyon geçiş de takibe alınmış özel otoyollarda çünkü kara yollarında herhangi bir icrai işlem başlatmıyoruz. Kara yollarından geçilen ücretler, kamu alacağı olduğu için orada zaten araç muayenede, noter satışında bir şekilde tahsil ediliyor ve yasal takip yapmıyoruz. Özel otoyollar, kamu alacağı olmadığı için orada yasal takip kanuna göre yapılıyor.
HGS süreci 2010’da başladı, 2018’de 10 kat olan ceza dört kata düşürüldü, 2022’de de ceza süreçleri 15 günden 45 güne uzatıldı. Kredi kartına bağlanan hiçbir HGS geçişinde sıkıntı yok. Sadece PTT’nin HGS hesaplarında yetersiz bakiyeler maalesef sıkıntı. e-Devlet üzerinden yapılan bildirimler, yine çok dikkatli takip edilmiyor.
Yaklaşık 1,5 ay önce KVKK’nin ‘Hiç kimse hiç kimsenin plakasını sorgulayamaz’ kararı var. Bunun üzerine bizim diğer sistemler üzerinden yapılan sorgulamalarda biraz aksama oldu. Bunu da görüştük, gideriyoruz. HGS etiketinin kullanılmıyor olması, araç sahiplerinin ve kullanıcılarının farklı olması karşılaştığımız problemlerdir. Yasal takibi durdurduk.
Sorularınızda ‘Yasal takibi durdurdunuz ancak ödenmişler ne olacak?’ dediniz. Usulüne uygun yapılmamış bütün ödemeleri geri iade ettireceğiz. Usulüne uygun yapılmamış olan icra takiplerinden bahsediyorum.
2025 için 25 bin tane dosyayı da tek tek incelediğimizi özellikle dikkatinize sunmak isterim. Yani bu noktada da bir şey kaçırmamaya gayret ediyoruz.
Bunları da kamu alacağı olarak adlandıralım, buna bir yasal düzenleme gerekiyor ve icra takiplerini kaldıralım. Bu bir alternatiftir. Yine ceza oranlarını düşürelim, bu da bir alternatiftir. Ödeme günlerini artıralım, bu da bir alternatiftir.”

Ulaştırma ve Altyapı Bakanı Abdulkadir Uraloğlu , Hızlı Geçiş Sistemi'nde ( HGS ) yasal takibi durdurduklarını ve usulüne uygun yapılmayan ödemelerin iade edilmesini sağlayacaklarını açıkladı. Uraloğlu, yarın Karayolları Genel Müdürlüğü (KGM) koordinasyonunda işletmecilerle toplantı yapılacağını bildirdi.
Bakanlıkta HGS'ye ilişkin açıklamalarda bulunan Uraloğlu, son günlerde otoyol geçiş ücretleri ve HGS konusunda basına ve sosyal medyaya yansıyan konuları hem Bakanlık hem de KGM olarak yakından izlediklerini söyledi.
Uraloğlu, "Kredi kartına bağlanmış olan hiçbir HGS geçişinde sıkıntı yok. Yasal takibi durdurduk. Usulüne uygun yapılmamış olan bütün ödemeleri iade ettireceğiz" dedi.
Otoyollarda araçların HGS etiketi veya plaka üzerinden tanımlandığını aktaran Uraloğlu, ücretlendirmenin de bu bilgiler esas alınarak yapıldığını kaydetti.
HGS bulunmadığında aracın plakası üzerinden tespit edilebildiğini belirten Uraloğlu, şu ifadeleri kullandı:
"Eskimiş etiketler ya da kirlenmiş, deforme olmuş plakalar varsa bu noktada bazı zorluklar yaşadığımız da oluyor. Mevcut sistemin yapay zeka destekli algılamasıyla beraber o plakayı tahmin ediyoruz, ona göre işlem yapıyoruz. Eğer burada bir yanılgı var ve bize bildirilmişse geriye doğru yapılmış olan bütün işlemlerin iptal edildiğini özellikle belirtmek isterim."
Uraloğlu, ihlalli geçişlerde vatandaşların sistemde kayıtlı telefon numaralarına 15 gün içinde SMS gönderildiğini söyledi. Bakiyenin yetersiz olduğu durumlarda da bildirim yapıldığını belirten Uraloğlu, vatandaşlardan araç plakalarıyla ilişkilendirilen telefon numaralarını e-Devlet veya HGS sistemleri üzerinden güncellemelerini istedi.
"Biz 15 gün içinde gerekli bildirimi yaptık, eğer vatandaşımızın eksik bakiyesi varsa veya plakası hiç HGS abonesi olmamışsa, 'süre geçti, sen geçemezsin' demiyoruz. 15 gün içinde bir HGS hesabı açar öderse yine hiçbir problem yok. Bunlar olmadı, 15. günden 45. güne kadar bir kat ceza uygulamasıyla yine aynı süreç devam ediyor. Yani vatandaşımız 45. güne kadar eğer öderse bir kat ceza uygulaması söz konusu. 46. günden sonra özellikle kamu-özel işbirliği otoyollarında vatandaşa en az 15 gün içinde bir tebligatla bildirim yaparak bu süreci yine durdurmayı maksatlıyoruz. Eğer bu tebligata rağmen bir işlem, bir ödeme, bir başvuru yapılmamışsa bu sefer olay esasında bizim de istemediğimiz avukatla takip sürecine kadar gidiyor. Burada ben özellikle söylemek istiyorum, bütün bu dediklerim yapılmış da vatandaşa yine bir şekliyle gitmişse biz de birebir takip ediyoruz ve bu sefer ilgili işletmeciye idari yaptırımlar uygulama noktasında da tasarrufta bulunuyoruz. Dolayısıyla bizim vatandaşımızdan beklediğimiz, otoyoldan geçtiğini, hesap bakiyesini bilmesi ama bunlar yoksa bizim bildirimlerimiz üzerine mutlaka gereğini yapması. Esasında SMS'le de e-Devlet üzerinden de bildiriyoruz. Bunları vatandaşlarımız takip ederse, biz de vatandaşımız da rahat etmiş olur."
Uraloğlu, daha önce herhangi bir plakaya ilişkin sorgulama yapılabildiğini, ancak bu uygulamanın yakın zamanda değiştiğini belirtti.
Değişikliğin Kişisel Verileri Koruma Kurulunun kararı doğrultusunda yapıldığını aktaran Uraloğlu, şunları söyledi:
"Kişisel Verileri Koruma Kurulunun (KVKK) yapılan şikayetler üzerine incelemesi sonucu, bunun doğru olmadığı, kişisel verilerinin ihlal edildiği noktasında bir karar alması ve o kararı da bizlere bildirmesi sonucu biz mecburen artık sadece ilgilinin bu sorgulamayı yapabilmesine imkan tanımış olduk. Öncesinde KGM'nin, PTT'nin, işletmecilerin sistemlerinden bunu yapabilirken artık KVKK kararıyla biz e-Devlet üzerinden yaptırma uygulamasına başladık. Dolayısıyla burada vatandaşımızın bir alışkanlığı, bir geçiş süreci söz konusu olduğu için tekrar böyle bir gündem oluşmuş oldu."
Uraloğlu, vatandaşların bildirimleri takip etmesinin önemini vurgulayarak sorunların çözümü için atılabilecek ilave adımları değerlendirdiklerini belirtti.
"Vatandaşlarımız daha duyarlı olsunlar. Biz de bu noktada daha ne yapılabilir, bunu özellikle sorguluyoruz. Amacımız vatandaşa asla ceza vermek, cezalandırmak değil. İşletmecileri, ihlaller avukata yani 4 kat cezaya gitmeden ne yapabiliriz konuşmak üzerine yarın tekrar bir topluyoruz. KGM koordinesinde yarın masaya oturulup değerlendirilecek ve toplantı yapılacak. Özellikle şunu da söylemek istiyorum, bu söylediğim çerçeve dışında bir davranışla karşılaşmış olan vatandaşlarımıza her türlü iletişim kapılarımız açık ve onlarla ilgili her türlü ilgi, alakayı göstereceğimizi özellikle belirtmek isterim."

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to staff during his first all-hands since returning to the company, while attempting to distance himself from the narrative that the White House and tech leaders helped him get his job back, according to reports from Bloomberg , The New York Times , and The Handbasket’s Marisa Kabas .
During the meeting, Huang reportedly called claims that President Donald Trump was directly involved in his reinstatement — an idea publicly promoted by Trump himself — “completely untrue.” He added, “Don’t think for a second politics played a role in the company. We are the most apolitical company,” according to Kabas .
Along with attempting to dismiss Trump’s involvement, Huang reportedly said he also didn’t return because he was a “tech bro” who was “above the law” or “above the code of conduct.” He added that, “no story has been more tortured than this one in human history,” Kabas reports . Instead, Huang said the Nvidia board “evaluated the entire situation,” while receiving assurance from the government that he posed no national security threat, according to the NYT .
Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on November 12th, following reports of affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two employees, including vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell. On Monday, Nvidia announced that it had reinstated Huang as CEO , president, and member of the board — a decision the White House said Trump was “totally involved in.” Trump also confirmed that he worked with Vice President JD Vance and other officials to bring Huang back. A swath of tech leaders, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and former White House AI czar David Sacks, were also in favor of Huang’s return .
In a post on Truth Social , Trump said that the government “has no reason to believe” Huang’s return poses a risk to national security, adding that the US attorney general “does not possess evidence” that he engaged in “unlawful conduct.” Nvidia is still facing an investigation over its accounting practices, according to Reuters . The company is also carrying out its own internal investigation surrounding reports that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy plot. Huang is set to testify before Congress on December 1st to answer questions about national security concerns, and Democrats are already planning to press Huang about his return, as well as Trump’s involvement.
Even after all this, Huang reportedly said he “doesn’t believe in succession planning.” He also acknowledged that he violated Nvidia’s code of conduct, adding that he is attending therapy daily, Bloomberg reports. “I made some terrible mistakes,” Huang said, according to the NYT . “I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids and of course, I hurt all of you.”
texts.https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2:
Huang acknowledges he violated code of conduct by having affairs, but denied Trump was instrumental in his return
Jensen Huang apologized to staff on Tuesday for the tumult he’s caused at Nvidia. The company’s CEO acknowledged he violated the code of conduct for having extramarital affairs, but pushed back on the reports that Donald Trump was instrumental in his reinstatement as chief executive.
“I made some terrible mistakes,” he said, according to a livestream reviewed by the New York Times . “I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids and, of course, I hurt all of you.”
The apology came one day after Huang returned as CEO of Nvidia , and less than two weeks after he was ousted from the role. Following a whiplash series of events, the company’s board of directors reinstated Huang on Monday, despite his admission that he’d had an affair. News reports allege the CEO had romantic relationships with two company employees and a suspected Chinese spy.
During Tuesday’s apology, Huang told staffers he was in therapy and that it was “not acceptable” that he violated the company’s code of conduct. In an impromptu speech to employees on Monday, Huang said he was “terribly sorry for putting all of you through all of this” and that he’s “going to be a better CEO the second time around”.
While Huang apologized for his affairs, he rejected narratives that he was a “tech bro” who was “above the law”, according to the New York Times. He added that it was “completely untrue” that Trump pressured Nvidia’s board to reinstate him. The board changed course, he said, because it “evaluated the entire situation” and “gathered facts”. Huang said Trump assured the board that he was not a national security threat.
The US government has been investigating whether Megaspeed , a Singapore-based company formerly run by Huang’s alleged ex-lover, Alice Huang (no relation), diverted Nvidia semiconductors to China in breach of export controls. US government officials have also raised concerns about Alice Huang’s alleged role as a Chinese asset.
Trump reportedly dialed into Nvidia’s Sunday board meeting to advocate for Huang’s return, according to Semafor . Nvidia’s board publicly said on Monday that it reached its decision to bring back Huang with “input from senior levels of the United States government”.
Huang potentially faces two congressional hearings next week, one before the House Foreign Affairs Committee and one before the Senate Banking committee. Gregory Meeks, a democratic congressman from New York and ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said on Tuesday that despite Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s CEO, a hearing should still take place.
“The American people deserve to hear publicly from Mr Huang about how potentially billions of dollars’ worth of our most advanced technology wound up in the hands of our greatest competitor, and what role this administration played,” Meeks said.
texts.https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/24/in-all:
After a whirlwind period during which Jensen Huang’s life fell apart and then came back together again, the Nvidia founder now wants his staff to know that he’s a changed man.
Huang held Nvidia’s first all-hands meeting on Tuesday since his reinstatement on Monday. During that meeting, CNBC reported that Huang struck a “remorseful tone” and told the crowd “I hurt all of you.”
The founder, whose extramarital affairs have been accused of jeopardizing everything from the stock market to U.S. national security, went on to describe how difficult the current moment is for him: “This is going to be the hardest company meeting I’ve ever done, and the second hardest meeting I have ever done,” Huang reportedly told staff .
“The hardest meeting I’ve ever done was with my wife,” he added.
The CEO admitted in the meeting that he had flouted Nvidia’s code of conduct , which he himself had largely devised. Huang emphasized that the code of conduct was still in effect, but that mitigating circumstances would matter a lot. As Wired reported Huang’s statement, it “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door.”
Huang told staff that he’s in therapy and also said that he was grateful for a second chance at the company.
The CEO is now walking a difficult tight rope between reasserting his authority over one of the world’s most powerful and influential companies, and conceding that he may have made some mistakes. He also tackled the difficult question of President Trump’s role in his restoration. The president reportedly called Nvidia’s board directly to lobby for Huang’s return, but in his talk, Huang downplayed Trump’s role
Huang thanked the administration on Tuesday for “providing Nvidia with quick access to intelligence that he said helped the board determine that the national security risks the company faced in reinstating him were low,” The Wall Street Journal writes .
Huang will likely need the administration’s support as he weathers an upcoming wave of congressional scrutiny from a newly Democrat-led government. The CEO is scheduled to appear for a public Senate Banking Committee hearing next week and, in the coming weeks, he will be called to appear for a number of different closed House hearings, including for the Intelligence Committee, the Foreign Affairs Committee, and the China Select Committee.

“Ay Tenli Kadın” şarkısıyla şöhreti yakalayan Ufuk Beydemir , birkaç ay önce sosyal medya hesabından yaptığı paylaşımla baba olacağını duyurarak hayranlarını şaşırtmıştı.
Hollandalı şarkıcı sevgilisi Sharon Kovacs mutluluk pozlarına da paylaşan Beydemir, bir kızı olacağını açıklamıştı.
Birkaç gün önce doğumun planlanandan haftalar önce başladığını duyuran şarkıcı, bu sebeple sevgilisinin yanına Hollanda'ya gitmişti. Birkaç gün önceki paylaşımında da 25'inci haftaya girdiklerini ve doğuma kadar hastanede olacaklarını söylemişti.
Beydemir bu açıklamasından 3 gün sonra baba oldu. 34 yaşındaki şarkıcı, kızlarına Ruby Umay adını verdiklerini açıkladı.
“Ruby Umay 25 hafta 3 günlükken aramıza katıldı” diyen Ufuk Beydemir, “Sharon da Ruby de iyi. Önümüzde yoğun bakımda geçecek uzun bir yol var ama kızımız daha ilk anından ne kadar güçlü olduğunu gösterdi. Bu zor günlerde dua eden, mesaj atan, iyi dileklerini gönderen herkese yürekten teşekkür ederiz. Hepsini okuduk, hepsi bize güç verdi” ifadelerini kullandı.
İlk kez baba olmanın mutluluğunu yaşayan Beydemir'in paylaşımına çok sayıda tebrik mesajı geldi.
Öte yandan Ufuk Beydemir, oyuncu İpek Filiz Yazıcı ile yaşadığı aşkla adından söz ettirmişti. Mutluluklarını 2022'de nikahla taçlandıran ikili, Roma'da evlenmiş iki ay sonra da Türkiye'de düğün yapmıştı. Yazıcı ile Beydemir, 2025 yılında yollarını ayırdı.

A jury has found Huawei guilty of stealing US trade secrets, as reported earlier by NBC News and Bloomberg . The verdict, handed down in a federal court in New York, concludes a years-long legal battle that accused the Chinese telecom giant of stealing source code and proprietary technology from several companies, including T-Mobile , Cisco, and Motorola.
The Department of Justice’s 2018 criminal indictment against Huawei came to light following the arrest of the company’s CFO, Wanzhou Meng , whom the agency accused of fraud. Though the indictment against Meng was eventually dismissed, she admitted to misleading banks over Huawei’s operations in Iran as part of a deferred prosecution agreement . The US government blacklisted Huawei in 2019 over national security concerns.
In total, the jury found Huawei guilty of 10 of 12 criminal counts, including money laundering, violating US sanctions, bank fraud, wire fraud, and conspiracy to defraud the US. The company was acquitted of engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice. Huawei’s sentencing is set for September 14th, 2027, where it may face “financial penalties including criminal fines, forfeiture, and restitution,” according to the DOJ.
“For over two decades, Huawei built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft, and deception,” Tysen A. Duva, the assistant attorney general of the DOJ’s criminal division, says in a statement. “Huawei’s crimes threatened the U.S. financial system, took advantage of American companies that compete honestly in the global telecommunications market, and undermined our national security.”
In a statement to NBC News, a Huawei spokesperson said the charges are “without legal or factual merit” and that it plans to appeal the decision. Huawei didn’t immediately respond to The Verge ’s request for comment.

A New York jury on Tuesday found Chinese telecom giant Huawei guilty of stealing trade secrets and other criminal offences, but acquitted it of a racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice. The verdict followed a three-month trial in New York in a case that adds to longstanding US efforts to curb Huawei's operations over alleged threats to national security.
A US jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei of stealing trade secrets Tuesday, but acquitted it of a more serious racketeering allegation, according to the Department of Justice.
The world's leading telecom equipment manufacturer, Huawei has been targeted by the Trump administration, which alleges a risk of it spying on behalf of the Chinese government.
The United States has previously urged countries not to use Huawei infrastructure for the rollout of new 5G mobile networks.
The verdict followed a three-month trial at a New York federal court, the US Department of Justice (DOJ) reported, with jurors finding Huawei guilty of 10 of the 12 criminal counts facing it – including bank fraud, conspiracy to steal trade secrets and conspiracy to defraud the United States.
"No person or company is above the law," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement. "For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft."
Beijing lashed out at the United States following Wednesday's ruling, accusing it of "suppressing" Chinese companies.
The Chinese government "firmly supports Chinese enterprises in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests", foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a news briefing, when asked about the Huawei conviction.
The jury did, however, acquit the company of racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice, a move Huawei said in a statement it "welcomed", adding that it "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years".
"We believe the government's remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit ... We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests," the statement continued.
The charges in part involved Huawei's business dealings with the government of Iran.
"Huawei repeatedly lied about the nature of its business in Iran, falsely telling banks, journalists, and the US government that it did not assist Iran's government, military, or intelligence community," DOJ said.
"Huawei lied about its activities in Iran to banks to obtain billions of US dollars and access to US-dollar clearing services, which enabled Huawei to be a sophisticated participant in a global marketplace for telecommunications services – in part because of its lies."
The equipment manufacturer was also accused of attempting to recruit employees of US telecoms firms and obtaining technological information from them in the process.
That data allegedly enabled Huawei to develop products similar to those of its competitors, which it then sold at lower prices, according to the original indictment.
"The misappropriated intellectual property included trade secret information and copyrighted works, such as source code and user manuals for internet routers, antenna technology, and robot testing technology," the DOJ said in a release.
Huawei even launched an internal programme offering bonuses to employees who obtained industrial secrets from competitors, prosecutors claimed.
"Today's verdict sends an unmistakable message: America will defend its businesses, protect its workers, and safeguard its national security against corrupt foreign corporations that lie, cheat, and steal to get ahead," Assistant Attorney General Tysen A. Duva said in a statement.

Sell-off signals investors are bracing for further volatility in key AI sector driving economic growth worldwide
Technology shares led a market retreat Tuesday as caution returned after Jensen Huang’s extraordinary return to Nvidia days after he was forced to resign, with investors bracing for further volatility in a key sector driving economic growth worldwide.
A day after Huang’s reinstatement as CEO drove Nvidia shares up more than 30%, adding more than $900bn to the firm’s market value, the euphoria dissipated as its stock lost almost 6% by Tuesday’s close.
Anthropic also slumped, giving up about 6.5% to $81.90, below its $83 price for last week’s IPO.
Monday aside, AI stocks had already sold off sharply throughout November on worries about profitability and the vast sums pumped into the sector.
By end of day in New York, the tech-heavy Nasdaq had shed 1.48% and the broader-based S&P 500 lost 0.5%, while the Dow was just into the green.
Europe’s main stock markets, which feature far fewer tech companies than their Asian and US rivals, finished a handful of percentage points lower after jumping Monday in line with Wall Street. The FTSE 100 went largely unchanged on Tuesday, closing down 0.13%.
Huang had resigned less than two weeks ago over extramarital affairs, reportedly with an alleged Chinese spy as well as a senior Nvidia executive before Donald Trump noisily declared he should be brought back.
“Jensen’s return takes away one of the biggest unknowns hanging over the AI trade,” said Charu Chanana, an investment strategist at Saxo Markets.
“He is not just Nvidia’s CEO; he is arguably the biggest salesman for the entire AI ecosystem. His relationships with customers, suppliers and capital providers are difficult to replicate,” she said.
But “Jensen Huang alone cannot support the AI trade in the long term,” said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.
“Nvidia’s stock price decline on Tuesday is to be expected after such a large rally in the previous session,” she added.
Analysts were in broad agreement that Huang’s return did not mean an end to investigations or the uncertainty that has clouded the AI trade for six months.
The company remains under scrutiny from investigators including at the FBI and on Capitol Hill for allegedly helping Chinese firms gain access to Nvidia’s top-line chips.
texts.https://www.wired.com/story/jensen-huang:
Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO signals that the chipmaker may have grown too important to the stock market for the US government to hold it accountable for national security lapses, intelligence and export-control experts warn WIRED. The move also undercuts the warnings Washington routinely issues to American companies and foreign governments about Beijing’s pursuit of US technology, they say.
Nvidia’s board brought back Huang on Monday, 11 days after he resigned amid revelations of extramarital affairs —one of them with Alice Huang, a woman US intelligence suspects has ties to China’s Ministry of State Security. The board said input from “senior levels of the United States government” left it confident that his return poses no national security risk .
President Donald Trump told The Wall Street Journal he lobbied the board directly and through intermediaries, and that Nvidia’s falling share price helped his case. The board acted before its own investigation of Huang had concluded, and while the Justice Department is pursuing a criminal probe of Megaspeed—a Singapore company Alice Huang once ran—over the alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China. Alice Huang is also under investigation , according to director of national intelligence Jay Clayton.
The experts tell WIRED they worry more about the precedent Huang’s return sets than about Huang himself. Some say the scrutiny now on him makes further compromise unlikely. But Beijing may already have gained insight into Nvidia’s chip designs and its private conversations with the White House and Congress, or, through Megaspeed, obtained the chips themselves, they say, and no one has publicly established what, if anything, it got.
Several want to know who gave the board its assurances and on what basis, and whether the government ran a counterintelligence damage assessment or simply made a political judgment. They also say the administration has repeatedly failed to enforce its own export controls, and that when intelligence concerns appear to yield to market pressure, US warnings about China start to sound negotiable, to Beijing’s benefit.
“If intelligence assessments are seen to be overridden, selectively interpreted, or publicly dismissed for political or commercial reasons, this could undermine long-term confidence in the independence of national security institutions,” says Tahlia Peterson, a cyber and technology research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a London defense think tank. “That would be damaging to US national security, and potentially advantageous to Beijing.”
Advisers briefed Trump at least twice on Alice Huang’s links to Chinese intelligence before the affair became public, and both times he played down their concerns, The New York Times reported Sunday . When the Journal asked him on Monday about Republican lawmakers who say Huang’s return endangers national security, Trump pointed to Nvidia’s rebounding stock.
“Some tech companies have become so big—and so important to the stock market—that Washington is reluctant to hold them accountable for national security lapses,” says Edward Fishman, director of the Council on Foreign Relations’ Maurice R. Greenberg Center for Geoeconomics.
Fishman sees a parallel in Wall Street’s slow reckoning with sanctions. “It took years of aggressive enforcement to get banks to take US sanctions compliance seriously,” he says. “We haven’t seen anything comparable in the tech sector, which helps explain why US export controls remain so weak and leaky.” Reinstating Huang on the administration's assurances before Nvidia’s own investigation has concluded “does not inspire confidence that meaningful enforcement is coming,” he says.
Emily Kilcrease, a former deputy assistant US trade representative who now directs the Energy, Economics, and Security program at the Center for a New American Security, says the administration’s record gives little reason to take those assurances at face value. “We cannot rely on the administration’s judgment, as it has repeatedly failed to enforce export controls over the past year,” she says.
On Monday, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist, and the administration has recently moved to tighten rules on China’s AI industry. But Kilcrease says it acted only under pressure. “Given the poor track record on export controls and their broader accommodationist stance toward China, it’s fair to ask whether they are willing to really enforce the new controls,” she says.
The board’s assurances appear to have come mostly from the Justice Department. Attorney general Todd Blanche allegedly told Trump and vice president JD Vance on Saturday that Huang was neither a target nor a subject of any department investigation, and that the department had no evidence he had broken the law or posed a national security risk, the Journal reports. Vance then reportedly sought assurances for the board that the administration did not consider Huang a threat and that he would not face criminal charges. Trump told the Times he also consulted Clayton before pushing for Huang’s return. (“I can’t do this and then all of a sudden have somebody get indicted,” he said.)
Nvidia did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
Whether Huang broke any laws is a separate question from whether Beijing gained anything through him. “Did [the assurances] reflect a counterintelligence damage assessment by the intelligence community or the FBI, or were they political in nature?” says Jessica Brandt, a senior fellow for technology and national security at the Council on Foreign Relations who previously directed the Foreign Malign Influence Center at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. “Lawmakers should press on that.”
Senior officials may have seen intelligence that isn’t public, so the assurances shouldn’t just be dismissed, says Sunny Cheung, a China studies fellow at the Jamestown Foundation. “However, we still don’t know who provided those assurances, what evidence they reviewed, or how they reached their conclusion, particularly when Nvidia’s own independent investigation remains unfinished,” he says.
Lawmakers appear to have seen little of that evidence. At a briefing this month by CIA director John Ratcliffe and Clayton that was scheduled to cover Iran, lawmakers pressed for answers about Huang, and the responses left some of them puzzled, according to the Times. A follow-up briefing for senior national security staff was postponed.
Cheung says the Ministry of State Security may not have needed Nvidia’s secrets to profit from the relationship. “From a counterintelligence perspective, I think people are too focused on whether Jensen handed over trade secrets,” he says. “China’s Ministry of State Security wouldn’t necessarily need Nvidia’s next-generation chip blueprints to benefit from access to him.” Insight into Huang’s direct conversations with the president, senior officials, and other top tech executives, along with his views on China and Taiwan and his role in Washington’s export-control debate, “could already be extremely valuable to Beijing,” he says.
Brandt sees the same mix of risks. “Information about Nvidia’s proprietary chip designs could help China advance its own chip design efforts,” she says. “Insight into Nvidia’s conversations with the White House and Congress could help Beijing anticipate where US export control policy is headed.” Investigators should also ask whether Alice Huang compromised Huang’s devices, what security clearance he held, and whether he still holds it, she says.
Huang successfully lobbied the Trump administration to roll back restrictions on Nvidia’s chip sales to China and negotiated a deal giving the US government a 25 percent cut of sales of certain chips approved for export there, the Times has reported . ​​​​​​New York'un Brooklyn bölgesindeki federal mahkemede jüri, Huawei 'yi karşı karşıya olduğu 12 suçlamanın 10'undan mahkum etti.
Şirket, örgütlü suç faaliyeti yürütmek amacıyla komplo kurmak ve adaleti engellemek suçlamalarından ise suçsuz bulundu.
Huawei ve üç iştiraki, örgütlü suç faaliyeti yürütmek amacıyla komplo kurma, banka dolandırıcılığı, elektronik iletişim yoluyla dolandırıcılık, yaptırımları ihlal etme, ticari sırları çalmak için komplo kurma ve adaleti engellemek amacıyla komplo kurma gibi suçlamalarla yargılanıyordu.
Huawei'den yapılan açıklamada, jürinin hükümetin şirkete yönelttiği organize suç faaliyetleriyle mücadeleyi öngören RICO Yasası kapsamındaki suçlamadan Huawei'yi beraat ettirmesinin memnuniyetle karşılandığı belirtildi.
Açıklamada, kararın söz konusu iddiaların olgusal dayanaktan yoksun olduğunu doğruladığı ve şirketin son sekiz yıldır sürdürdüğü tutumun haklılığını ortaya koyduğu ifade edildi.
Hükümetin yönelttiği diğer suçlamaların da hukuki ve olgusal dayanaktan yoksun olduğuna inanıldığı vurgulanan açıklamada, ticari sırlarla ilgili hükümetin gündeme getirdiği beş uyuşmazlığın tamamının son 20 yılda çözüme kavuşturulmuş hukuk davaları olduğu kaydedildi.
Açıklamada, hiçbir mahkemenin Huawei'yi fikri mülkiyeti kasıtlı olarak kötüye kullanmaktan sorumlu tutmadığına ve şirketin ticari sırların kötüye kullanılması nedeniyle hiçbir zaman tazminat ödemeye mahkum edilmediğine işaret edildi.
Huawei'nin açıklamasında, "İlgili mahkeme kararlarını kapsamlı şekilde inceleyecek, haklarımızı ve çıkarlarımızı korumak için gerekli tüm hukuki adımları atacağız" ifadeleri kullanıldı.
ABD Adalet Bakanlığı, 2018'de Çin'in ekonomik casusluk ve fikri mülkiyet hırsızlığı faaliyetleriyle mücadele amacıyla "Çin Girişimi" adlı programı başlatmıştı.
Huawei hakkındaki dava da aynı yıl gündeme gelirken şirketin kurucusu Ren Zhengfei'nin kızı ve Mali İşler Direktörü (CFO) Meng Wanzhou , ABD'nin İran yaptırımlarını ihlal ettiği gerekçesiyle 2018'de Kanada'da gözaltına alınmıştı.
Meng, ABD'li savcılar tarafından, Huawei'nin İran'daki ticari faaliyetleri ve Hong Kong merkezli Skycom şirketiyle ilişkisi konusunda HSBC başta olmak üzere bankaları yanıltmakla suçlanmıştı.
Savcılık, Huawei ile bağlantılı Skycom şirketinin 2007-2014 yıllarında İran'da faaliyet gösterdiğini ve ABD yaptırımlarını ihlal ettiğini öne sürmüştü. Meng'in ise Huawei ile Skycom arasındaki sahiplik ilişkisini gizleyerek bankalara iki şirketi birbirinden bağımsız kuruluşlar olarak tanıttığı iddia edilmişti.
Huawei, ABD'nin ulusal güvenlik ve dış politika endişelerini gerekçe göstererek Amerikan şirketlerinin teknoloji ve ürün satışlarını kısıtlaması kapsamında 2019'da ticaret kara listesine alınmıştı.
Meng, ABD Adalet Bakanlığı ile vardığı ertelenmiş kovuşturma anlaşması kapsamında 2021'de Çin'e dönerken hakkındaki suçlamalar düşürülmüştü. ABD'nin eski Başkanı Joe Biden döneminde ise 2022'de Çin Girişimi programı sona erdirilmişti.
Meng hakkındaki davanın kapanmasına rağmen Huawei'ye yönelik ceza davası devam etmişti.

ABD merkezli çip üreticisi Nvidia 'nın üst yöneticilik (CEO) görevine yeniden atanan Jensen Huang , şirkete dönüşünün Başkan Donald Trump 'ın baskısıyla gerçekleşmediğini söyledi.
New York Times'ın (NYT) haberine göre Huang, yaptığı konuşmada yönetim kurulunun durumu bütünüyle değerlendirmesi ve gerçekleri ortaya çıkarması sonucunda görevine döndüğünü belirtti.
CEO'luk görevini yeniden üstlenmesinin ardından çalışanlardan özür dileyen Huang, şirketin davranış kurallarını ihlal ettiğini kabul etti.
Huang, "Çok kötü hatalar yaptım. Lori'ye (eşi Lori Huang) sadakatsizlik ettim. Çocuklarımı ve elbette hepinizi incittim" ifadelerini kullandı.
Terapi gördüğünü açıklayan Huang, davranışları nedeniyle yönetim kurulunun şirketteki geleceğini değerlendirmek zorunda kaldığını ve bu sürecin sonunda 12 Kasım'da istifa ettiğini aktardı.
Trump'ın yönetim kuruluna kendisini yeniden göreve getirmesi için baskı yaptığı iddiasını reddeden Huang, dönüş kararının kurulun değerlendirmesine ve gerçeklerin ortaya çıkarılmasına dayandığını vurguladı.
Trump ise daha önce Nvidia Yönetim Kurulu'nu Huang'ın yeniden CEO olarak atanması konusunda ikna ettiğini söylemişti.
Nvidia Yönetim Kurulu, Huang'ın yabancı istihbarat faaliyetinin hedefi olduğuna yönelik haberler üzerine 8 Kasım'da bağımsız soruşturma başlatıldığını açıklamıştı.
Soruşturma, Huang'ın Pekin yönetimine bilgi aktardığı öne sürülen Çinli iş insanı Alice Huang ile yakın ilişkisi bulunduğuna ilişkin haberlerin ardından başlatılmıştı.
Şirket, 12 Kasım'da Huang'ın başkanlık, üst yöneticilik ve yönetim kurulu üyeliği görevlerinden derhal geçerli olmak üzere ayrıldığını duyurmuştu.
Nvidia, dün Huang'ı yeniden şirketin başkanlığına ve üst yöneticilik görevine getirmişti.

The US Army is scrambling to contain any potential lead pollution that could spread if an old stockpile of explosives blows up.
The US Army is moving ahead with plans to detonate the nation’s stockpile of lead azide at an ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, at approximately 9:00AM CST on Wednesday . The Verge reached out to experts on what to expect, and will keep this post updated.
There are 68 drums holding about 9,700 pounds of lead azide, an unstable chemical compound created to detonate munitions like grenades. The US started using lead azide as a primary explosive almost a century ago before “moving away” from it about 15 years ago because of how difficult the material is to store and transport, Robert Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), said in a Tuesday press briefing . At that point, the US transferred its remaining stockpile of lead azide to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. Lead azide will explode at 350 degrees Celsius (662F). But it is also sensitive to flame, friction, or sudden shock, including fluctuations in temperature.
Some of the material on site in Iowa is more than 60 years old. The material can crystallize as it degrades over time, becoming unstable enough to explode even at ambient temperatures . The Army noted some deterioration of the material in 2009 — but not any “dangerous crystallization” at the time, according to Cekada.
The chemical was stored in liquid form, embedded in sawdust and burlap bags inside the drums. Water and ethanol were also added to the containers to keep the lead azide from freezing in the winter. But during a March inspection, Cekada said ATF noticed “significant crystallization on the exterior of the barrels.” That made the material too unstable for them to open the barrels to add more water and ethanol, Cekada said. Removing a lid might cause the barrels to detonate.
Officials have been trying to figure out what to do with the crystallized lead azide since that alarming March inspection. The Army initially hired a contractor to safely dissolve the chemicals but canceled the contract earlier this year, according to reporting by The New York Times . Using a chemical neutralization agent “proved to be an unsafe method,” Army Col. Aaron Teller, commander of the 71st Explosive Ordinance Disposal Group, said at the Tuesday briefing, because crystallization on the outside of the barrels made it too risky to open the lids.
“Everyone that we’ve spoken to through their experience has determined that this is the only safe path forward,“ Cekada said at the briefing. If they leave the chemicals as is, he said, they’re still at risk of exploding. “It’s not a matter of if, it’s a matter of when.”
Compared to an uncontrolled, spontaneous explosion, a controlled detonation is supposed to limit the amount of lead dust unleashed on surrounding communities and the environment. Still, the dust plume could reach as far as 100 miles away from the site. The Army has released maps showing where lead dust is expected to travel based on its modeling.
The last time the Army disposed of lead azide this way at a comparable scale was in 1977, according to Teller. At the time, they detonated 7,000 pounds of the material in Colorado in open air “with zero mitigation.” Even then, 75 percent of the lead particulate stayed on site, Teller said at the briefing. The Army now believes it can “significantly reduce” the spread of that last 25 percent of lead using walls made up of four 16,000-gallon water tanks to capture lead particulate and hopefully prevent it from escaping into the atmosphere.
The 80-year-old earth-covered magazines holding the lead azide are cracked and deteriorating, Teller noted, and they are likely to break open after the detonation. To prepare, they’ve covered it with tarp and a special containment screen for lead. They also plan to flood it with 2 feet of foam to capture particulate pollution. Adam Telle, Acting Secretary of the Army, also said the Army has set out “state of the art gel blocks in huge quantities all around to ensure that we absorb as much of this blast as we possibly can.”
Last week, the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club sought a court order to stop the explosion from taking place, pending an Environmental and Health Impact Statement and an investigation into alternatives to detonating the material. President Donald Trump chimed in on social media, calling for a pause until a federal appeals court gave the Army the green light after previously granting a temporary stay. The court on Monday denied the emergency motion to stop the explosion, clearing the way for the Army to move forward.
The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services (Iowa HHS) recommends that anyone in potentially affected areas stay indoors and keep windows shut for 24 to 48 hours after the detonation. Iowa HHS also suggests switching off HVAC systems that might bring outdoor air inside or set them to modes that recirculate air, and using an air purifier with a HEPA filter.
FEMA is helping relocate Middletown residents and others within a voluntary 5-mile evacuation zone. People who are pregnant, children, and individuals with chronic diseases should evacuate the affected areas, Sean Kaufman, principal deputy assistant secretary for preparedness and response at the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response, said at the briefing. “Outside of that area, if you’re close to that proximity and you’re uncomfortable, I think you need to do what you need to do to take care of your family,” Kaufman said.
There is no “safe” level of exposure to lead, a neurotoxin that poses health risks when inhaled or ingested. Kids are at increased risk because their brains are still developing and are also more likely to touch contaminated surfaces and then stick their fingers in their mouths. But most adverse health effects — which can include fatigue and gastrointestinal upset alongside impacts on brain development — are connected to chronic lead exposure rather than as a result of a one-off event.
“It is likely this exposure will not result in any observable acute clinical signs,” Will Sander, associate professor of preventive medicine and public health at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, says in an email to The Verge. “Overall, the risk is minimal, and there should be no long-term concerns.”
“The Army has done this before a long time ago and took lead measurements afterward that were low but hazardous (in my opinion),” Chris Kohler, an adjunct instructor at Indiana University who is an expert on hazardous waste, environmental remediation, and chemical hygiene, says in an email to The Verge . “The detonation will spread lead in the atmosphere. Not a desirable outcome.” Kohler and other experts say it’ll be important to continue monitoring the explosion site and surrounding areas to see if there needs to be any more remediation.

Residents warned to stay indoors amid conflicting information about how far the dust plume could travel
The US Army is set to detonate 68 barrels – five tons – of lead azide at an ammunition plant in rural Iowa on Wednesday morning, after delays and conflicting information about how far the toxic lead dust plume could travel after the explosion.
That controlled blast has been scheduled for 10am ET on Wednesday, the day before the Thanksgiving holiday.
“Inaction is no longer an option,” Army Maj Gen Eric Shirley, the commander of the operation, said at a press conference in Middletown, Iowa, on Tuesday. “It would be irresponsible for us to not take the determined, consensus-based course of action moving forward.”
Federal officials on Tuesday said mitigation measures had been put in place, including barriers around the blast zone to capture much of the dust, but warned that residents in the vicinity should be prepared to evacuate.
“We don’t believe that the public should be in a panic,” said Adam Telle, acting secretary of the army. “Our goal is to keep as much of it as we can here on our Iowa Army Ammunition plant to prevent it from traveling.”
Telle said weather ⁠conditions on Wednesday morning were expected to be “ideal to protect public health and safety across the region” and stressed that a “controlled, mitigated, detonation” was “far preferable to an uncontrolled spontaneous detonation” of the unstable material.
State officials, environmental groups and residents have sharply criticized federal authorities over what many have described as a “communication failure” about the operation.
In a statement, Iowa senator-elect Josh Turek welcomed the army’s “long-overdue press conference” about Wednesday’s operation and vowed to “continue asking questions about how we got here” when he joins the chamber in January.
“There is no excuse for such a failure of transparency and communication, especially when the health and safety of the public is involved,” said Turek, who was born with spina bifida, which he attributes to his father’s exposure to Agent Orange during the Vietnam war. “Iowans should have had a full and clear understanding of the health implications of this operation, especially as children, pregnant women, and those with chronic illness are being advised to stay away from the affected area.”
Earlier on Tuesday, the army released new maps showing the projected plume path moving south-west of the Iowa army ammunition plant in Middletown, stretching through a south-eastern portion of the state before extending into northern Missouri.
The army sent an emergency notification to cellphones on Tuesday confirming the time of the controlled explosion – and warning that some people within 5 miles south-west of the plant may be evacuated.
The “imminent threat alert” told those up to 20 miles away to remain indoors with windows closed “to avoid airborne lead dust, noise and vibration”.
On Tuesday, the outgoing governor, Kim Reynolds, issued a proclamation of disaster emergency for Des Moines, Lee and Van Buren counties. Additionally, Reynolds said, she was deploying up to 100 soldiers from the Iowa national guard to support with public safety efforts.
Earlier in the day, the governor announced her support for the planned detonation after speaking with military leaders, including US defense secretary Pete Hegseth.
“I trust the army will do everything in its power to protect the people who could be affected,” she said in a statement.
The army said it had set up additional “blast barriers” around the bunkers where the lead azide will be detonated. It also said it would apply ballistic gels and foams to absorb the lead dust and douse the explosive materials with thousands of gallons of water.
The decision to proceed came after a federal appeals court cleared the way for the detonation to take place after the date had been changed three times after an outpouring of public concern. Environmentalists sued to stop the detonation, arguing that the planned explosion had not been issued permits correctly.
An attorney for the environmentalists emphasized that their legal challenge centers on the validity of the Environment Protection Agency permit – not the army’s decision to move forward with the detonation under the emergency provision.
The army said it needs to blow up the stockpile to prevent a possible chain-reaction explosion, which would be more dangerous.
The order to go ahead came after an extraordinary intervention by Donald Trump, who said on social media that in addition to the court’s go-ahead, he wanted Rob Sand, Iowa’s governor-elect, to approve the detonation.
Sand, a Democrat who does not take office until January, has said the decision is fully up to the president’s administration.
Evacuated residents will be notified by phone once they may return home, the Des Moines Register reported .
The army and the Iowa department of health and human services are recommending that those in the area take protective measures. Those include closing all windows and exterior doors; turning off or placing heating, ventilation, and air conditioning systems in recirculation mode; avoiding unnecessary travel; and cleaning indoor and outdoor surfaces that may be contacted by children.

US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.
Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.
Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."
Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.
Trump has said he would consider pardoning Huang for any potential criminal activity, though he does not think it will come to that.
"It's always an option, I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary," Trump told the New York Post in an interview published on Tuesday.
With Huang rescue, Trump riskily ties his political fortunes to Nvidia
The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China.
In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations" .
But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.
"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.
Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about any chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.
"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.
Huang reportedly apologised to Nvidia employees on Tuesday, the day after returning to the company as chief executive, saying he made "terrible mistakes" and is now in therapy for 90 minutes per day.
The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
On Monday, Trump said he spoke to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang .
Republican congressman Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang".
Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".
Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions".
Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".
US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal

Defence lawyer Brian Heberlig makes closing arguments at the Huawei Technologies trial at Brooklyn federal court on November 17.
Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US.
In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.
Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.
Huawei said , external the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis", adding that it would "take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests".
Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.
However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.
Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.
Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.
During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge.
"For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in statement , external .
"Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable."
However, defence attorney Brian Heberlig said it was by dint of hard work that Huawei's business had expanded with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff.
Following the verdict, Heberlig told the BBC that Huawei was gratified that the jury had rejected the racketeering charge.
"The RICO [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act] count that alleged that Huawei was a corrupt organisation, with a corporate culture and policy of committing crime. That was, in our view, a significant overreach, and the jury soundly rejected it," he said.
"Of course, we have mixed emotions about the rest of the verdict ... [we] thought that Huawei was deserving of acquittals across the board."
Sentencing is planned for September 2027. Heberlig said there will be "significant advocacy" to achieve the lowest sentence possible. Following that, he said he fully expects Huawei to appeal.
"If I know Huawei, that fight will continue, and the company's not going to rest until it's pursued every last argument it can through appeal, and hopefully, ultimately toward vindication," he said.

Several employees say rapid speed at which algorithms work means mistakes can happen at greater scale
Meta employees have expressed concern at the company’s push to replace human moderators with artificial intelligence, claiming the technology is leading to mistakes with the potential for sweeping political consequences.
The social media company, which owns Facebook and Instagram, has been experimenting with AI-driven moderation for years, first introducing it in 2017 to filter out violent extremist content.
This March, Meta announced it was “transforming our approach” by rolling out “more advanced AI systems” to moderate content across its apps, framing the change as a way to improve enforcement.
Several Meta employees said that behind the scenes this push to AI was accompanied by mass layoffs across the company, severely affecting staff responsible for reviewing content on its platforms.
One described Meta’s content moderation as now operating with “skeleton teams”, some cut by at times half or two-thirds of their staff.
“It’s been really a mess,” they said, adding that on several recent occasions they had gone to discuss an issue with a specific content moderation team, only to find that entire team was now gone.
Meta has long sought inexpensive ways to moderate the vast volumes of content posted each day to its platforms. It has faced legal action from former outsourced content moderators in Kenya, who described struggling with PTSD and severe mental health issues after being paid as little as $1.50 (£1.13) an hour to view and evaluate extremely graphic content that users attempted to post.
Meta employees say AI systems that the company is now using struggle with nuance, especially in languages other than English, and frequently remove content that should not be taken down.
“You are trying to gut all human reviewers, which are kind of essential for making these nuanced decisions and policy decisions,” said one employee. “Of course there are going to be mistakes that are going to happen.”
The employee said that because algorithms were automated, and worked at greater speed than humans, these mistakes could happen at a greater scale. The employee said Meta was removing lower-paid contractors, such as those in Kenya, and the full-time employees who would handle more complex content moderation.
Once a post is taken down, there is far less recourse for the affected accounts than before. “Even if you know someone at Meta, it’s still very difficult to get through to someone who’s actually going to be able to help you, especially if it’s a highly nuanced case,” the employee said. “It’s so much more difficult now.”
The growth in AI moderation comes as researchers monitoring online censorship have noticed a new phenomenon: sudden restrictions on Instagram and Facebook accounts, often during pivotal political moments.
Some of these have been isolated occurrences, such as Meta’s suspension of the US No Kings account in the run-up to the US midterm elections. Others have amounted to “mass takedowns”, unfolding over the course of days and hitting dozens of social media accounts.
It is a growing phenomenon, the consequences of which could “shape the political future of entire nations”, said Martha Dimitratou, the founder of the group Repro Uncensored, which monitors digital censorship.
Repro Uncensored has tracked these takedowns in Brazil, the EU, Turkey and the US. The Guardian reported on a wave of account takedowns on Meta platforms late last year, affecting accounts posting queer content and those dedicated to reproductive health across Europe. Accounts backing the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, were restricted or suspended from Instagram in the feverish days of Brazil’s election runoff, according to Repro Uncensored. Meta said most of the Brazilian takedowns were to comply with valid court orders or electoral regulations.
The numbers of affected accounts appear to be rising: Repro Uncensored documented 210 incidents of account takedowns on Meta in 2025, and 657 in the first six months of 2026 .
Meta employees who spoke to the Guardian said AI moderation had a role in such incidents as algorithms worked faster, and with less nuance, than human reviewers. “The effect of it is you see these sweeping takedowns,” one said.
But they also said they could not rule out political considerations in how Meta’s algorithm was designed. Meta’s systems are opaque, even to its employees. They are a combination of LLMs – large language models, like chatbots – and older algorithms that filter content.
There are “thousands of levers and factors that weigh into how things are ranked”, said one employee, and these change constantly.
The employees suggested that at times Meta’s use of AI had allowed the company to obscure more controversial decisions it makes in how it moderates political content. They gave the example of how Meta made adjustments to its algorithm in late 2023 that drastically limited the number of posts that appeared from people in Palestine.
The company rejected allegations of bias and said it had previously carried out independent human rights due diligence in relation to the conflict, and since 2022 had been working to implement the resultant recommendations, including by “introducing a system that detects and prioritises content to moderators most likely to understand that particular Arabic dialect”.
One employee said AI offered “plausible deniability”. It afforded “exactly the kind of ambiguity that they hide behind”, they said.
In response to questions from the Guardian, a Meta spokesperson said: “Everyone on our platforms is subject to the same set of rules, and any claims of enforcement based on political affiliation or advocacy are baseless.
“While we have long used AI to help enforce our community standards, earlier this year we began experimenting with more advanced AI systems that can more quickly and accurately catch violations with fewer mistakes. The latest tests show that on average these systems make 13% fewer mistakes than humans when enforcing against violating content, while finding 10% more actual violations – and we give people opportunity to appeal decisions if they think we’ve got it wrong.”

Abelardo de la Espriella to take control of an operation involving scores of security personnel trying to free at least 20 hostages
Colombia’s president has arrived at the scene of an hours-long standoff between security services and gunmen holding at least 20 people hostage inside a supermarket in Cartagena, a popular tourist city.
Abelardo de la Espriella’s motorcade arrived in Cartagena on Tuesday night, Agence France-Presse reported, where he will ostensibly take control of a operation involving scores of officers, the navy and special forces.
About 30 people were initially seized by the armed men early on Tuesday morning, but by nightfall, 10 hostages – five of them elderly women – had been released, police said.
Before arriving in Cartagena, the right-wing president said that, despite the context of growing violence perpetrated by criminal groups involved in the country’s decades-long armed conflict, the hostage-taking appeared to have stemmed from a botched robbery carried out by “common criminals”.
The past few days have been particularly challenging in the South American country, with a car bomb and a drone attack killing one person and leaving nearly 30 injured.
The supermarket where the hostages are being held is just six miles from the old city and its 500-year-old fortress walls overlooking the Caribbean. Hundreds of thousands of visitors are drawn to Cartagena every year.
The gunmen reportedly arrived at about 8.30am local time at an Éxito supermarket in La Castellana neighbourhood and, according to Colombia’s president, the group planned to rob an armoured cash-in-transit vehicle that was due to collect the previous day’s takings from the store.
After spotting the movement on security cameras, employees reportedly alerted the national police, who surrounded the supermarket.
“My son is there,” Jacob Perez, the father of one of the workers reportedly held hostage, told Agence France-Presse. “He didn’t leave work and he’s not answering his phone. I think they took it from him,” he said.
Customers were also believed to be among the hostages. The five people initially released were “older women”, according to De la Espriella.
Footage shared on social media showed dozens of people rushing out of the supermarket, while local media outlets showed snipers positioned on nearby buildings in what appeared to be a standoff between the armed men and police.
De la Espriella, known for his populist rhetoric and an “iron fist” approach to crime – he sometimes wears a gun on his waist and has posed beside the bodies of people killed by police – has been in office for just over three months, and said the hours-long standoff at the supermarket “will turn out well for the hostages, but I’m not so sure it will turn out quite so well for the hostage-takers”.
He addressed the case at a press conference in Villavicencio, about 684 miles inland, where he was dealing with the aftermath of an attack on Monday night in which a car bomb was detonated outside the headquarters of the Meta departmental government.
More than 20 people were injured and a security guard was killed, and the president attributed the attack to a dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc).
“Narco-terrorism is desperate because we are confronting it decisively. It intends to intimidate us and force us to retreat in search of another false peace process,” the president said, referring to the landmark 2016 peace deal between the government and the Farc – whose signing marked its 10th anniversary on Tuesday.
Internationally recognised for substantially reducing violence, the deal alone could not bring the decades-long armed conflict to a definitive end. Subsequent administrations were slow to implement the agreement, which was rejected by Farc dissidents and other rebel factions.
In the early hours of Monday, in another part of the country, gunmen believed to belong to the ELN, an armed group that never signed a peace deal, used drones to drop bombs on the local police command in the city of Cúcuta. Instead they hit homes and injured three civilians, including an 18-month-old baby.
Although drone attacks by criminal groups have become increasingly common, it was the first time they had targeted a departmental capital.

Kilmar Ábrego García has left the United States of his own volition, his lawyers confirmed on Tuesday, with the Department of Homeland Security confirming that he was travelling to Spain.
The Salvadorian immigrant was at the center of a months-long legal battle since he was deported to El Salvador in March 2025 by the Trump administration, in defiance of a court’s protection. He was held in Cecot, a notorious anti-terrorism mega-prison .
He was ultimately returned to the US after a decision by the supreme court three months later. Since then, Ábrego has been fighting a second deportation to a series of African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officials.
The Washington Post reported earlier on Tuesday that he negotiated a deal with federal authorities to depart the US voluntarily in order to avoid being forcibly removed.
In a statement, the US senator Chris Van Hollen, who has advocated for Maryland resident Ábrego and who met with him in El Salvador last year, described him as a “free man” and referenced Ábrego’s agreement with the Trump administration.
“While the Trump Administration had been pursuing their vindictive prosecution against Kilmar and desperately trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation,” Van Hollen said. “I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution.”
The 31-year-old has an American wife and child and has lived in Maryland for years, but he immigrated to the US illegally as a teenager. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the US under Immigration and Customs Enforcement supervision, but he was not given residency status.
He was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported to a Salvadorian prison in what an official later called an “administrative error”. Facing public pressure and a court order, the Trump administration brought him back in June 2025, but only after securing an indictment charging him with human smuggling in Tennessee. A federal judge dismissed that case in May, finding that the justice department’s pursuit of criminal charges was designed to punish Ábrego García for challenging his deportation. The government is appealing.
The Trump administration vowed to deport him to a third country, threatening to send him to Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana and, most recently, Liberia.
“We will always admire his remarkable courage in staring down and defeating a vindictive prosecution instigated by the highest reaches of the Justice Department,” one of Ábrego García’s attorneys, Sean Hecker, said in a statement provided to the Washington Post . “He, in turn, is grateful to those who stood by him.”

Kilmar Ábrego García, whose deportation last year to El Salvador sparked a bitter deportation battle, has left the US for Spain.
After the government admitted it had wrongfully sent Ábrego García to his home country, he was returned to the US to face human trafficking charges, which were later dropped. The administration then continued its attempts to send him to other countries, including Uganda and Ghana.
His deportation and return became a flashpoint in the debate over President Donald Trump's immigration agenda.
Ábrego García, who is married to a US citizen and lived in Maryland, came to the US illegally from El Salvador as a teenager.
Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, visited Ábrego García while he was in the notorious Cecot prison in El Salvador in 2025 and advocated for his release.
"A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego García to rot in a Salvadoran gulag," Van Hollen said in a statement on Tuesday. "Today, Kilmar is travelling to a country of his choice, a free man - unharmed and with dignity."
In a statement, Ábrego García's lawyer said his departure was "temporary" as he had "many options to return to the United States".
"We don't expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland," the statement said.
"Where he goes from here, where he chooses to settle for the next two years while he waits out the end of this administration, will be his choice, not the administration's choice."
The BBC has contacted the US Department of Homeland Security for comment.
Ábrego García was arrested in 2019 alongside three other men and detained by federal immigration authorities. A judge granted him protection from deportation to El Salvador at the time, citing the risk of persecution by a gang there.
In March 2025, the Trump administration deported him to El Salvador, where he was held in Cecot, a prison known for its harsh conditions. The US Supreme Court then ordered the government to facilitate his return.
The administration admitted that he was deported in error and brought him back to the US where he was set to face human trafficking charges. A federal judge dismissed the case, saying Ábrego García had been charged for political reasons.
For months, he was locked in a battle over deportation with the government.
Ábrego García had repeatedly said he would be willing to be deported to Costa Rica, and the Costa Rican government had agreed to accept him as a refugee and provide him with legal status.
After reports emerged that the administration was considering sending him to Uganda, a judge barred the government from deporting Ábrego García to a third country.
At one point the Trump administration requested that the judge lift the order so that Ábrego García could be deported to Liberia, CBS reported.

Colombia's President President Abelardo de la Espriella said on Wednesday that around 20 hostages being held by gunmen in a supermarket in Cartagena had been rescued. Security forces earlier entered the scene of the hours-long siege after several explosions were heard.
Colombian security forces stormed a supermarket in the Caribbean city of Cartagena early Wednesday, successfully rescuing around 20 hostages being held by armed men, Colombia's President President Abelardo de la Espriella said.
Espriella said one hostage-taker was killed in the rescue operation which began after several explosions were heard and security forces moved into the building after an hours-long siege.
Authorities said 10 of the roughly 30 hostages initially held had been released after hours of negotiations, including several elderly women.
Gunmen earlier seized dozens of hostages at a supermarket in Cartagena on Tuesday, triggering a tense standoff with police, troops and special forces who surrounded the building and cut power to the area.
Authorities said the gunmen had attempted to rob an armoured vehicle before fleeing into the supermarket and taking about 30 people hostage as police closed in.
Reuters images showed heavily ⁠armed military and police gathered outside the supermarket.
President Abelardo de la Espriella travelled to Cartagena as the crisis unfolded and met security commanders at the scene to ostensibly take control of a massive operation involving scores of officers, the navy and special forces.
"Thirty people were kidnapped, five of ​whom have already been released. They are ‌older women," De la Espriella had said earlier from the city of Villavicencio, where he traveled following an overnight ‌bombing there.
"All the capabilities of our various security forces, ​have now been deployed, including special units," he added.

China has launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft with a Pakistani astronaut on board, the first time a foreign national has flown to its Tiangong space station.
Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, lifted off on Wednesday morning with Chinese crewmates Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39, from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China.
Hours earlier, crowds gathered for a send-off ceremony, many filming on their phones.
Following the launch, the capsule separated from its rocket and reached its planned orbit.
It is the first joint flight of Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's crewed space programme.
Thousands of kilometres away, Pakistanis watched the ascent on television at home and in restaurants, chanting slogans in praise of God and of Pakistan-China friendship. Scientists at the national space agency's headquarters followed the launch live.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called the mission a source of national pride and an inspiration for the country's youth.
"This is not just one astronaut's journey, but the journey of 240 million Pakistanis," he wrote on X. He thanked Beijing for including a Pakistani astronaut and said the flight extended the two countries' close ties into space.
Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, speaking to reporters at the agency, thanked President Xi Jinping, China's leadership and its scientists and engineers, and said he hoped the flight would be the start of broader cooperation.
Asked whether Pakistan could one day send astronauts on its own, he replied: "Certainly that day will come."
Iqbal said Ali carried the Pakistani flag on his uniform, lifting his compatriots' hopes and technological ambitions into orbit. "The sky is no longer our limit; it is our launching pad," he said, calling the mission an inspiration for young Pakistanis hoping for careers in science and technology.
The flight stems from an agreement the two countries signed in February 2025. The Chinese media reported that the crew will carry out more than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests.
Ali, who is on a short-term mission, will run an experiment on photosynthetic cyanobacteria before returning to Earth aboard Shenzhou 23. Ali and Wu are making their first spaceflight. Tang has flown twice before and is set to become the first astronaut to board Tiangong three times, according to state broadcaster CCTV.
At a press conference on Tuesday, Tang said differences in language, culture and psychology had made training together harder, but that the effort was paying off.
Ali showed as much by speaking Mandarin and citing a line of Chinese poetry about climbing higher to see farther. "It's like my daily training. Day after day, reaching new heights," he said.
Switching to English, Ali said he hoped cooperation would grow from one astronaut on one flight to multiple joint missions and eventually to the Moon, Mars and beyond.
China is preparing to land astronauts on the Moon by 2030. The United States is widely seen as its main rival, with NASA aiming to put astronauts on the lunar surface in 2028.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia, who was wrongfully deported to El Salvador last year as part of United States President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, has self-deported to Spain.
Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national, voluntarily departed on Tuesday after months of legal opposition to a second deportation, this time to one of various African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security officials.
